doc.title: Eddie Metz Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 3, 2015

title: Gus Johnson, Connie Kay and subdividing the beat
summary: Hearing Erskine with Maynard and Kenton, learning from Gus Johnson's closed hi-hat and comparing Connie Kay's even eighths with triplet-feel drummers.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Oh my God it was — and they didn’t want to let them off the stage. In fact Maynard’s band was sitting on the stage watching them. And they looked at Maynard and Maynard went, “go ahead, play another one, I don’t care.” And it was just killer. And so Peter was with Maynard at that time. So it was more rock & roll Maynard Ferguson. And so to see him go and play straight ahead jazz, I did hear him when he was very young with Kenton when he was 19 years old or something. Just a powerhouse of a player. But now he can do all of this delicate stuff. And it’s just again, intensity of the beat when you’re playing soft and doing that. And I picked that up from, I saw Gus Johnson one time. We were watching them on that video. It went to piano solo and he went just to hi-hat, closed hi- hat, and nothing else. And it still was swinging. And I was like it can be done, yes it can be done. You don’t have to play all that extra stuff. When it comes down to the quarter note just play it. Now the subdivision might be different. A drummer like Connie Kay from the Modern Jazz Quartet played his jazz being very even eighths. Did you ever notice that? Okay. Or if you got to somebody like Jake Hanna or Buddy Rich or Max Roach or any of the bebop drummers, their beat kind of went [claps]. So there was that in-between that mystified me most of the time. It was like well Connie Kay can get away with it playing straight eighths in a jazz sense, and these other guys can do it with a triplet feel, which is the jazz-swing trio — the first and third note of a triplet — right? [scats] The shuffle feel without the middle note. The ride cymbal pattern for drummers, that’s where that comes from [claps]. So if you’re subdividing [claps]. Now it’s hokey when you go [claps]. But when you have it in the ride beat and it’s constant and it’s steady, I think it helps everyone just not worry about where the beat is. And then they can play the bass or the piano. How do they do it. I have no idea how they do it. I mean Rossano, all the notes and everything. I’m just hitting things with pieces of wood, you know? He’s over there actually — but I have to give the support. So it all comes back to the quarter note again.
